title: From Ambient Documentation to Clinical Intelligence — Chaitanya Asawa, Abridge
talk_summary: Abridge's engineering lead describes how they keep quality, latency, and cost high in a high-stakes clinical agent product: eval-as-operating-system with clinician-calibrated LLM judges and rubrics, plus decomposing work into narrow workflows with small post-trained models and cheap gating before expensive model calls. The transferable core is rubric-based judges, staged rollout, and cheap-trigger gating to avoid burning frontier models on every event.

takeaways.technique: Rubric-based LLM judges calibrated by domain experts
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of a single golden answer, independent clinicians author rubrics of required elements, a separate clinician adjudicates, a fourth QAs, then an LLM judge semantically matches agent output against rubric elements for hill-climbing.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we had independent physicians create a rubric... a separate physician that actually adjudicated it... a fourth clinician do QA on these rubrics

takeaways.technique: Multiple orthogonal judges instead of one verifier
takeaways.what_they_do: They run several specialized judges (clinical quality, boundary/adversarial, safety, tone/style) because a single generator-verifier gap is too small to trust one judge.

takeaways.technique: Cheap gates trigger expensive models only on real events
takeaways.what_they_do: Rather than running a heavy model every few seconds on the live conversation, they use a chain of cheaper/faster gates to detect the right events, then hand off to larger models for the expensive end-to-end matching.
takeaways.evidence_quote: a number of different gates that are cheaper and faster that let us trigger actually larger models and hand off to them

takeaways.technique: Decompose into narrow workflows and post-train/route small models per section
takeaways.what_they_do: They split the note into sections and use smaller specialized models per section instead of one frontier model for everything, because narrow problems don't need frontier intelligence.
New capabilities go internal benchmark -> alpha trusted users -> beta/A-B -> full rollout with ongoing monitoring, because offline evals never fully represent production.

takeaways.technique: Online signals as eval feedback loop
takeaways.what_they_do: They capture edit diffs, thumbs up/down, star ratings, and free-form text as online signals feeding the eval loop, not just offline benchmarks.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we also have a lot of online signals whether how you're editing the clinical note and your typical thumbs up, thumbs down
